analysis.one_liner: Lets families sue private detention companies at least $5 million when a detainee dies.
analysis.headline: Introduced July 22, 2026 with 3 Democratic cosponsors, the bill sits in the House Judiciary Committee with no hearing, vote, or further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let the family of anyone who dies in a privately run detention facility that holds people under a federal contract sue the company and its employees in federal or state court. Damages would start at $5 million on top of economic losses, with punitive damages available, and the company would be responsible for its employees' actions with no immunity defense. Today the bill has only been introduced and sent to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Families and estates of people who die in private detention facilities — mainly immigration detainees and federal prisoners held by contractors — would gain a federal right to sue with a guaranteed minimum payout of $5 million plus economic and punitive damages, and could also bring claims in state court. Detainees themselves gain indirectly, since facilities facing real liability have a financial reason to prevent deaths.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families of people who die in private detention

how_it_helps.text: Creates a private right of action so the family or estate of a person who dies in a private detention center can sue the facility's officers, employees, and the company itself in federal district court or state court.

Guarantees statutory damages of at least $5 million plus economic damages, with punitive damages as appropriate — a payout floor that does not depend on proving the company's net worth or the victim's earning power.

Makes the private detention company vicariously liable for its employees' conduct and bars employees from raising absolute or qualified immunity as a defense, closing the escape hatches that often defeat lawsuits over deaths in custody.

Applies to any private entity holding people under a federal contract for alleged civil, criminal, or immigration violations, covering the private companies that run immigration detention and federal prison beds.

analysis.who_pays: Private detention companies and their employees would pay the damages, and the companies' insurers would bear much of the cost. Because these facilities operate on federal contracts, the companies would likely raise the prices they charge the government to cover the added liability, passing part of the cost to taxpayers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private detention companies, their insurers, taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The flat $5 million minimum per death, with uncapped punitive damages on top, would sharply raise the cost of private detention contracts, and companies would likely pass those costs to the federal government — meaning taxpayers help fund the payouts.

The bill only covers privately operated facilities; families of people who die in government-run prisons and detention centers would get no comparable federal remedy, creating a two-track system based on who operates the facility rather than how the person died.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For a family that loses someone in a private detention facility, the bill offers a concrete remedy where current law often leaves them with little recourse against the company. The tradeoffs are real: a guaranteed multimillion-dollar floor per death would be priced into federal detention contracts, and the remedy is limited to private operators, leaving deaths in public facilities with no equivalent route. The accountability goal is legitimate, but the design is blunt, and as introduced the bill has no realistic path to a vote this Congress.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: Rep. Derek Tran introduced the Private Detention Corporate Accountability Act of 2026 on July 22, 2026, joined by three Democratic cosponsors.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary, the committee that would consider it before any floor vote.
No hearing, markup, or vote has followed, and the bill remains pending in committee while this Congress is still in session.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained or lost yet. The bill has not moved past its committee referral, so private detention companies currently face no new liability — and the families the bill is meant to help have gotten no remedy.

for.name: Rep. Derek Tran
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create federal wrongful-death liability for private detention contractors.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on July 22, 2026; no hearing, markup, or floor scheduling has followed.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred yet; all four sponsors are Democrats in a House controlled by a 223-seat Republican majority, so the bill's prospects so far track party lines.

industries.industry: Private prison and immigration detention companies
industries.note: Companies that hold detainees under federal contracts would face a minimum $5 million payout per detainee death plus economic and punitive damages, with the company liable for its employees and no immunity defense available. Facing that liability, they would raise contract prices, buy more insurance, or exit federal detention work.

analysis.trajectory: With a 223-seat Republican House majority, only three cosponsors, and no committee action since referral, the bill is very unlikely to get a hearing or a floor vote; it will most likely sit in the Judiciary Committee until this Congress ends on January 3, 2027, and die there.
